questions.question: What distinguishes supervised learning from unsupervised learning?
options: Supervised learning uses labeled data (input paired with correct output); unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabeled data
Supervised learning never requires any data at all
Unsupervised learning is always more accurate
There is no meaningful difference between them
questions.explanation: Supervised learning requires examples with known correct answers (labels) to learn from, while unsupervised learning discovers structure in data without any labels provided.

questions.question: A team wants to group similar customers for a marketing campaign, with no predefined 'correct' grouping. Which category does this fall into?
options: Supervised learning, because customers need to be labeled first
Unsupervised learning, because it finds patterns/groups without a predefined correct answer
Reinforcement learning, because it requires a reward signal
This isn't a machine learning problem at all
questions.explanation: Grouping data without predefined correct labels (clustering/segmentation) is a classic unsupervised learning task — no labeled 'correct group' is needed upfront.

questions.question: A data science team says a new ticket-classification feature needs 10,000 labeled examples. Which question best evaluates whether this is a real requirement?
options: Can we just skip labeling and hope it works?
Is this genuinely a supervised learning task, and if so, how was the 10,000 number derived — who will label them and how will labeling quality be validated?
Why do we need machine learning for this at all?
Can we replace labeled data with random data instead?
questions.explanation: Confirming the task truly requires supervised learning (labeled data) and understanding how the specific data volume estimate was derived helps distinguish a well-reasoned requirement from an inflated or unexamined one.
